# squatch-dsp - full context

> A small real-time C++17 sound engine for guitar effects: the Block/Arena/parameter core, limiter, noise gate, RBJ EQ and the Squatch Tuner, with thin hosts (JACK, a web page, WebAssembly in the browser). No fetched dependencies; make test runs ASan/UBSan/TSan suites including an allocation and lock watch.

Every file linked from [llms.txt](llms.txt), inlined in the same order (directories as file listings). Secret-shaped files (`.env*`, keys, credentials) and generated or vendored directories are never included. Generated by project-kit `llms/generate.py`; do not edit by hand.

<!-- SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT -->
# squatch-dsp

A small real-time sound engine in C++17 for guitar effects: each block is written once and runs
on a Raspberry Pi, a microcontroller, in a browser and in desktop plugins, with a thin host for
each. Nothing in the audio path allocates, locks, does I/O or throws, and the tests prove it for
every block.

It holds the core (the `Block` interface, a memory arena, parameters with smoothing and a
lock-free queue), four effect blocks, the Squatch Tuner, and each of them as a desktop plugin.
[ROADMAP.md](ROADMAP.md) says where it is going.

**The Squatch Tuner** is developed here, in [`blocks/tuner/`](blocks/tuner/), and published on
its own as [squatch-tuner](https://github.com/squatch-stack/squatch-tuner): the easy-to-embed
copy, with a **[browser demo](https://squatch-stack.github.io/squatch-tuner/)** you can try
with a guitar or a microphone.

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `include/squatch/dsp/` | the core: `Block`, `Arena`, `Setup`, `ParamDesc` and `Smoother`, `ParamQueue` (single producer, single consumer), `Latest` (newest-value snapshot), `DenormalGuard`, `Span`, `Chain`, and the heap-free factory by type id (`registry.hpp`) |
| `contracts/` | one control contract per block (`cc.squatch.control/1`): ids, keys, ranges, tapers, meters, identity. `tools/build-contracts` generates the C++ tables (`include/squatch/dsp/contracts/`) and the plugin list from them; see [contracts/README.md](contracts/README.md) |
| `include/squatch/dsp/blocks/`, `src/` | blocks: `Limiter` (lookahead, true-peak, with drive and output trim), `Gate` (noise gate with PiPedal's controls; ranges settled with the browser rig), `Eq` (RBJ low shelf, peak and high shelf), `Cabinet` (impulse response convolution with no added latency: a direct head and a uniformly partitioned FFT tail, on our own radix-2 `Fft`), `TunerBlock` (the tuner behind the `Block` interface) |
| `blocks/tuner/` | the Squatch Tuner: header-only core, measurement bench and [results](blocks/tuner/RESULTS.md) |
| `hosts/` | thin hosts: `clap/` (the desktop plugins: CLAP, and VST3 and AUv2 through clap-wrapper; [hosts/clap/README.md](hosts/clap/README.md)), `jack/` (the live tuner; the live rig, gate to limiter as one client; a loopback latency probe), `web/` (its page and a streaming bridge), `wasm/` (the tuner in the browser), `daisy/` (Daisy Seed3 firmware: passthrough, the gate to limiter chain with cycle counts, a latency probe, and a Neural Amp Modeler A2-Lite model running in real time on one core; [hosts/daisy/README.md](hosts/daisy/README.md)), `common/`, `tests/` |
| `tests/` | a small test runner, the real-time watch, double-precision references, golden renders |
| `bench/`, `results/` | CPU cost per block ([results/bench-mac.md](results/bench-mac.md)) |
| `docs/benchmarks/` | measured results with their method and how to repeat them: [A2-Lite on a Daisy Seed3](docs/benchmarks/daisy-seed3.md) (46.5% of one Cortex-M7 for the amp, 66.4% for the whole chain) |

## Rules

- **Real-time safe.** `process()` and `set()` never allocate, lock, do I/O or throw. All memory
  comes from the `Arena` in `prepare()`. `make test` checks this for every block, with hooks on
  operator new/delete, malloc/free and pthread and os_unfair locks.
- **C++17, with no exceptions and no RTTI in the core,** so the same code builds for a Cortex-M7
  and an ESP32-S3.
- **No fetched dependencies in the core.** Anything third-party is vendored, pinned and reviewed.
  There are no package managers and no build-time downloads. The plugin wrappers (`hosts/clap`)
  build against MIT/BSD code pinned by commit in `hosts/clap/deps.lock`, fetched once by
  `tools/fetch-plugin-deps`, never by the build.
- **Every block is checked against a reference:** a plain double-precision version of its
  definition, plus a golden render that catches any change of sound.
- **Small functions:** cyclomatic complexity of at most 10, at most 60 lines and 5 parameters per
  function (`make lint`), and conventional commit subjects.

The block contract (input and output, in place, block sizes, what `set()` may do) is at the top
of [`block.hpp`](include/squatch/dsp/block.hpp), with what version 2 added for plugin hosts:
`get()` for state and meters, channel layouts (mono, mono to stereo, linked stereo), `tail()`,
identity and version, and descriptors with a stable key, taper, steps and labels, and a role
(parameter, bypass or meter).

## Build and test

`clang++` or `g++`, and `make`. `lizard` is only needed for `make lint`.

```sh
make test       # ASan + UBSan unit, reference, golden and real-time tests; TSan for the queue
make lint       # complexity limits (lizard)
make bench      # writes results/bench-<machine>.md
make ci         # lint, a standalone compile of each header, the -O3 library, the tests
make golden     # rewrite tests/golden/*.inc, only after a deliberate change of sound
make live       # the live tuner and test tone: CoreAudio on macOS (nothing to install), JACK elsewhere (libjack-jackd2-dev)
make rig        # the JACK rig and latency probe; NAM_CORE=<NeuralAmpModelerCore checkout> adds the amp
make wasm       # the tuner's browser demo into build/web-demo (needs Emscripten)
make wasm-test  # the demo in Node and in headless Chrome, against exact test tones
make contracts  # regenerate the C++ parameter tables (and LV2/WAM/OSCQuery/MIDI-CI into build/contracts)
make plugins    # the desktop plugins into build/plugins/bundles (needs cmake and ninja)
make plugins-install   # copy them into $HOME/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins
make plugins-check     # sanitizers, clap-validator, VST3 validator, pluginval, auval
```

The Makefile uses clang++ where it exists and g++ otherwise; `CXX=...` overrides it. Where
ThreadSanitizer cannot run (a Pi 5's 47-bit address space), use `make test HOST_SAN=`.

## Adding a block

1. Write its contract, `contracts/<key>.params.json` (copy one), and run `tools/build-contracts`.
2. Put the header in `include/squatch/dsp/blocks/`, the code in `src/`, and declare the class
   `final : public Block, public contracts::<Name>Contract`: that brings the `Param` enum, the
   descriptor table `kParams`, `params()` and `kInfo`. `set()` clamps through the descriptor and
   smooths anything that would click; `get()` returns what `set()` kept, and each meter's newest
   value. Override `supports(Layout::Stereo)` only for a linked stereo path of its own.
3. Take every buffer in `prepare()` from the `Arena`. If an allocation returns null, stay silent in `process()`.
4. Support `in == out` and any `n` from 1 to `maxBlock`. Report `latency()` if the block delays the signal.
5. Keep filter state clear of denormals with `flushDenormal()` on the S3, which has no FTZ mode.
6. Write the reference in `tests/reference.hpp`: a plain double-precision version of the definition.
7. Add `tests/test_<block>.cpp` with behaviour tests, error against the reference and a golden render.
   Run `make golden` once, then check the new `.inc` file.
8. Add the block to `rtBlocksNeverAllocateOrLock` in `tests/test_rt.cpp`, to `registry.cpp`, and a row
   to `bench/bench.cpp`. For a plugin, give the contract an `auSubtype` and `features`.
9. `make ci` passes (and `make plugins-check` for a plugin), then commit with a subject like
   `feat(<block>): ...`.

## How this repository is published

squatch-dsp is developed in a working tree that also holds planning notes and scripts for our own
test bench. `tools/export-public dsp` publishes everything else here, file for file, and writes
`EXPORTED`: a SHA-256 for each published file. CI fails if a published file is
edited here directly (`tools/export-public dsp --verify .`). The same tool writes squatch-tuner
from this repository (`tools/export-public tuner`), and squatch-tuner's CI checks its copy of
the tuner against this repository's main branch, so the tuner has one source.

Issues and pull requests are welcome. A merged change is applied upstream and comes back with
the next export. Commit messages here carry no Co-Authored-By trailers, and commit dates are in
UTC (`TZ=UTC git commit`).

## Support this work

If this is useful to you, you can support its development through
[GitHub Sponsors](https://github.com/sponsors/squatch-stack).

<!-- SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT -->
# Contributing to squatch-dsp

Thank you for helping. Every change comes in as a pull request and is reviewed before it lands.
This page says what belongs here, how to shape a pull request, and what the checks look at.

## What belongs here

squatch-dsp is a **library**: a real-time sound engine in C++17. It holds:

- the block core (`Block`, `Arena`, parameters, control contracts) and the blocks built on it;
- their tests, references and golden renders, and the benchmark;
- the Squatch Tuner's source (`blocks/tuner/`, also published on its own as squatch-tuner);
- thin reference hosts that show the library in use (the web demo, plugin adapters).

It does not hold applications, products, device firmware, bench scripts or anything that needs
an account, a key or a download to build. If you are unsure whether something fits, open an
issue first.

## A good pull request

- **One change.** A fix, a feature, a refactor or a documentation change, not several. Refactors
  go in their own pull request, ahead of the change that needs them.
- **Small.** Aim for under 400 changed lines. Over 1000 needs a reason in the description (a
  maintainer then adds the `large-change` label); generated files are not counted.
- **Tested.** A behaviour change comes with a test that fails without it. A new block follows
  "Adding a block" in the [README](README.md).
- **Checked locally.** `make ci` runs what CI runs: `lint headers lib test`.
- **Commit subjects** follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/):
  `type(scope): summary`, at most 72 characters, with type one of `feat fix docs chore ci build
  test refactor perf style revert`. Say why in the body when it is not obvious. No `fixup!`,
  `squash!` or `WIP` commits in the final branch.

## What the checks look at

On every pull request (`.github/workflows/quality.yml` and `ci.yml`):

| Check | Limit |
|---|---|
| Cyclomatic complexity per function (`make lint`, lizard) | at most 10 |
| Function length | at most 60 lines |
| Parameters per function | at most 5 |
| Shell scripts (shellcheck) | no findings |
| Commit subjects (`tools/pr-shape`) | the format above |
| Pull request size (`tools/pr-shape`) | notice over 400 lines, fails over 1000 without `large-change` |
| Standalone headers, library, tests | pass under ASan + UBSan and TSan, with the real-time allocation and lock watch |

Nothing here is lowered to make a pull request pass: fix the code instead.

## Your machine

This repository installs nothing on your machine and changes no configuration: there are no hooks
to install, no package managers and no downloads at build time. The checks above run in CI; run
`make ci` yourself when you want them locally (it needs a C++17 compiler, make, and `lizard` for
the lint step).

## How a pull request lands

squatch-dsp is published from a development tree that also holds work that is not public yet.
Once a pull request is approved, a maintainer applies it there and it comes back here in the
next publish, credited to you. The `EXPORTED` file lists every published file; a pull request
may edit them, and CI reports which, but it only enforces `EXPORTED` on `main`.

Contributions are accepted under the MIT licence of this repository.

<!-- SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT -->
# squatch-dsp roadmap

## Goals

- **Write each effect once.** A gate, a drive or a reverb should sound the same on a Raspberry
  Pi, on a microcontroller pedal, in a browser and in a desktop plugin, because it is the same
  code. Each target gets a thin host; the blocks do not know which one they run in.
- **Real-time safe everywhere.** No allocation, locks, I/O or exceptions in the audio path, and
  a test that proves it for every block.
- **Checked, not assumed.** Every block has a reference to match (a double-precision render of
  its definition, or an established implementation such as NAM Core for amp models) and a
  golden render that catches any change of sound.
- **Small enough to trust.** C++17 without exceptions or RTTI, no fetched dependencies, small
  functions, and measured CPU cost per block on each target.

## The block interface

Every block implements one small interface (`include/squatch/dsp/block.hpp`, version 2):

```cpp
struct Block {
  virtual void prepare(const Setup& s, Arena& mem) = 0;  // rate, max block, layout; all memory taken here
  virtual void process(const float* in, float* out, int n) = 0;  // real-time safe, mono
  virtual void reset() = 0;                                // clear state, keep memory
  virtual void set(ParamId id, float value) = 0;           // clamped and smoothed inside the block
  virtual float get(ParamId id) const = 0;                 // what set() kept; a meter's newest value
  virtual int latency() const { return 0; }                // samples, for aligning parallel branches
  virtual int tail() const { return latency(); }           // samples after the input goes silent
  virtual bool supports(Layout) const;                     // Mono, MonoToStereo; Stereo if linked
  virtual void processChannels(const AudioIO& io, int n);  // any declared layout
  virtual Span<const ParamDesc> parameters() const;        // from the block's control contract
  virtual const BlockInfo& info() const;                   // type id, name, version, state version
};
```

Other threads change parameters through a single-producer queue, and blocks that only measure,
such as the tuner, publish their readings through a lock-free snapshot and as meters. A block's
parameters come from its control contract (`contracts/`), which also drives the LV2, WAM,
OSCQuery and MIDI-CI descriptions, so a preset reads the same on every target.

## Milestones

1. **Core and first blocks** (done). The `Block`, `Arena` and parameter core; a lookahead
   true-peak limiter, a noise gate and a three-band EQ; the Squatch Tuner as a block, with a
   live JACK host on a Raspberry Pi and a WebAssembly host in the browser.
2. **A microcontroller host.** The same blocks on a Cortex-M7 board (Daisy Seed), with the
   round-trip latency and the CPU per block measured on the board.
3. **Amp models.** A lean inference engine for NAM models with fixed memory, checked against
   NAM Core's output, on the Pi and on the microcontroller.
4. **Cabinets and routing.** Cabinet impulse responses (partitioned convolution), a fixed-size
   graph for series and parallel routing with latency alignment, a shared preset format and
   click-free preset switching. An LV2 plugin that hosts a whole board.
5. **More blocks.** Compressor, drives, envelope filter, delay and reverb, each with its
   reference and golden render.
6. **Browser and desktop.** The whole engine as WebAssembly in an AudioWorklet, and as desktop
   plugins. Started: the limiter, gate, EQ, tuner and cabinet are CLAP, VST3 and AUv2 plugins
   (`hosts/clap`), checked by clap-validator, the VST3 validator, pluginval, auval and sanitizer
   legs. Next: a native GUI, LV2 from the same contracts, and the iOS AUv3 spike.

## Open questions

- A small FFT of our own for convolution, or a vendored one: decided by measurement.
- Oversampling for the drives, 2x or 4x per block: measured for aliasing against CPU.
- The parameter-smoothing policy, and the control map for MIDI.

FILE: docs/benchmarks/daisy-seed3.md    [Docs: Daisy Seed3: a Neural Amp Modeler on one Cortex-M7]

# Daisy Seed3: a Neural Amp Modeler on one Cortex-M7

Measured on 2026-10-16 and 2026-10-17. Plain summary: the A2-Lite model from NAM Core's example A2 runs in real time on
a
single Daisy Seed3 core, using **46.5% of the chip** by itself and **66.4% on average (69.3% in the worst second)**
inside a
chain of gate, drive, amp and limiter, with no late or overrunning audio blocks. Everything marked **measured** was read
off the
board's cycle counter or from the linker; **estimate** and **inference** are marked where they appear. The firmware is
in
[hosts/daisy](../../hosts/daisy/README.md) (MIT), and this note says how to repeat every measurement.

## Contents

1. [Board and settings](#1-board-and-settings)
2. [The model](#2-the-model)
3. [How it was measured](#3-how-it-was-measured)
4. [Result: the amp alone](#4-result-the-amp-alone)
5. [Every variant we measured](#5-every-variant-we-measured)
6. [The whole chain, with audio](#6-the-whole-chain-with-audio)
7. [Memory](#7-memory)
8. [Round-trip latency](#8-round-trip-latency)
9. [What did not help](#9-what-did-not-help)
10. [What is untested](#10-what-is-untested)
11. [How to reproduce it](#11-how-to-reproduce-it)

## 1. Board and settings

| | |
|---|---|
| board | Electrosmith Daisy Seed3 (STM32H750IB, Cortex-M7 with FPU, 128 KB internal flash, 128 KB DTCM, 512 KB AXI SRAM) |
| clock | 480 MHz core |
| sample rate | 48 kHz |
| block size | 32 samples (also 16, 48 and 64 for the plain chain and latency images) |
| budget | one block lasts 320,000 cycles at 32 samples: 1,500 blocks a second |
| firmware | squatch-dsp `hosts/daisy`, libDaisy `facb66c7` plus two patches, built `-O3` (libDaisy `-Os` for the amp images) |
| compiler | Arm GNU Toolchain 15.3.Rel1, GCC 15.3.1 |
| samples | 32-bit float; the amp is float32 end to end, no integer kernel |

"% of budget" below is the cycles a piece of work takes divided by 320,000. At 100% the work takes the whole block and
audio
breaks.

## 2. The model

The amp is the **A2-Lite** submodel of `example_models/A2.nam` in NeuralAmpModelerCore (MIT, Steven Atkinson;
<https://github.com/sdatkinson/NeuralAmpModelerCore>, commit `0b3d3c97`, file sha256 `2d2d7445...fcf4ca`). That file is
a
"slimmable" container; the smaller submodel is a WaveNet with 3 channels and 23 dilated layers.

- 1,871 weights (7.5 KB in flash as float literals), receptive field 6,347 samples.
- 1,731 multiply-adds per sample, so 55,392 per 32-sample block.
- It is NAM Core's own example model; its MIT notice is in
  [hosts/daisy/THIRD_PARTY.md](../../hosts/daisy/THIRD_PARTY.md).
- The kernel (`hosts/daisy/nam/a2lite.hpp`) is our own code for this chip: fixed sizes, no heap, no libm, weights and
  state in
  static memory. `tools/nam_to_header.py` regenerates the weights header from the pinned model; CI checks that it
  matches.

## 3. How it was measured

All timings come from the Cortex-M7's cycle counter (DWT `CYCCNT`, a 32-bit counter running at the core clock), read
just
before and just after the work. No external instrument, no estimate from a datasheet.

- **Warm-up.** The model starts from silence and its biases settle over the receptive field, so before anything is
  recorded the board runs two receptive fields of silence through it (397 blocks). The same warm-up is how the images
  refuse to
  start audio if one block costs more than 90% of the budget.
- **150 steady-state blocks.** After warm-up the board feeds the model a fixed pseudo-random noise (a small linear
  congruential generator, amplitude 0.3) one 32-sample block at a time from the main loop, with no audio running, and
  records the
  cycles each of 150 blocks took (150 x 32 = 4,800 samples). Reported: mean, minimum and maximum. Running with no audio
  means a
  kernel that is over budget cannot starve the serial port.
- **Parity recording.** The same 4,800 input samples and the 4,800 output samples are sent over USB serial as raw float
  bits.
  The Mac then runs NAM's network in 64-bit floats (`hosts/daisy/tools/a2_reference.py`, straight from the `.nam`
  weights,
  fed the board's exact input bits) and scores the board's output as **ESR**, the error-to-signal ratio:
  `10 log10(sum of squared error / sum of squared reference)` in dB. More negative is better. The pipeline's gate is
  -100 dB.
- **Bit-exactness.** For variants that claim not to change the arithmetic, the pipeline also demands that all 4,800
  output
  samples equal the plain kernel's output on the board, bit for bit.
- **Negative control.** `nam_bench.py --selftest` adds `xbreak`, a variant with the output scale 1% off. It must be
  rejected. In
  every sweep it was (ESR -40.0 dB against the -100 dB gate, 0 of 4,800 samples equal), so a variant passing the gate is
  evidence rather than a gate that passes everything.
- **With audio.** The chain images run real audio callbacks on the board's audio clock and report, once a second, mean /
  99th percentile / worst callback cost as a share of the block, and counts of late and overrunning callbacks. Windows
  are
  one second; the first few are dropped.
- **Stack.** The unused DTCM below the stack is painted with `0xA5A5A5A5` at the top of `main`, and the lowest word that
  no longer
  holds the paint is read once a second. Not counted: the few hundred bytes the startup code uses before `main`.
- **One board, one compiler.** Everything was measured on one Seed3 with GCC 15.3.1. We have not tried a second board or
  compiler.

## 4. Result: the amp alone

**Measured** on the board, final code, 150 blocks of 32 (2026-10-17):

| | cycles per 32-sample block | % of budget | cycles per sample | cycles per multiply-add |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| plain kernel we started from | 329,950 | 103.1% | 10,311 | 5.96 |
| **final kernel (fused tiles, state in DTCM, head over a sliding window)** | **148,656** | **46.5%** | **4,646** | **2.68** |

- Evidence: `docs/benchmarks/data/daisy-seed3/nam-bench-final-sweep.csv` (the board's cycle counts, ESR and sample
  counts), and
  `hosts/daisy/tools/nam_check.py` for the board-against-Mac comparison.
- Minimum 146,336 and maximum 154,790 cycles over the 150 blocks.
- Accuracy: ESR **-123.9 dB** against the float64 reference, largest sample error 5.4e-08. The final kernel's output is
  **bit-identical to the plain kernel's on the board: 4800 of 4800 samples**.
- The same kernel built for the Mac is bit-identical to the plain kernel at block sizes 7, 16, 28, 32, 33, 48, 64 and
  100
  (measured on the Mac). Board against the Mac build (column `note` of
  `docs/benchmarks/data/daisy-seed3/nam-bench-final-sweep.csv`): 234 of 4,800 samples bit-identical, the rest differ in
  the last bits
  because the two compilers fuse multiply-adds differently; both have the same ESR against the reference.
- The plain kernel, at 103%, does not run in real time. The kernel is 2.2 times faster.

What the kernel does differently (from the code, and the counters in section 5):

1. It computes all three output channels of a tile of 4 frames together, with 12 accumulators in registers, so each
   loaded
   history value is used three times; the weights are repacked `[input][tap][output]`.
2. The activation is `max(z, 0.01 z)`, the same value for every finite input and free of branches.
3. The residual stream is stored straight into the next layer's ring buffer: no copy per layer.
4. The whole model object (rings, scratch, weights copy) lives in DTCM, the chip's zero-wait-state memory.
5. The head (a 16-tap convolution over three channels) works on 4 frames and two taps per pass.

Why a tile of 3 outputs by 4 frames: on this core a floating-point multiply-add does not overlap with a load.
Micro-benchmarks
on the board (**measured**, 1,000 passes with data in DTCM): 12 independent multiply-adds cost 12 cycles; 12
multiply-adds
plus 7 loads cost 19; 12 loads alone cost 8. So a pass costs the multiply-adds plus about one cycle per loaded word, and
the
way to go faster is fewer loads per multiply-add, not a different layout.

## 5. Every variant we measured

All rows are **measured** on the board with the pipeline in section 3. A kernel built from a different tree has a
slightly
different code layout, and the same source compiled to different cycle counts in different trees (the plain kernel took
351,737 cycles in the first experimental tree and 329,950 in the clean one), so **compare rows within a table, not
across
tables**. "The plain kernel" is the first, straightforward float32 kernel; a variant is "bit-identical" when all 4,800
recorded
output samples equal its output on the board. The `results.csv` files of the two 2026-10-17 sweeps are in
[data/daisy-seed3](data/daisy-seed3); the earlier sweeps' CSV files were not kept, and their figures (5.3, 5.4) are the
pipeline's tables as recorded at the time.

### 5.1 Final code, one sweep (2026-10-17)

Evidence: `docs/benchmarks/data/daisy-seed3/nam-bench-final-sweep.csv`; command: `hosts/daisy/tools/nam_bench.py
--selftest`.

| variant | what | cycles/block (min, max) | % budget | cycles/MAC | ESR dB | kept |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| base | plain kernel, rings and state in AXI SRAM | 329,950 (min 325,200, max 337,014) | 103.1 | 5.96 | -123.9 | baseline |
| fused+dtcm | fused tiles, state in DTCM | 154,393 (min 152,618, max 159,980) | 48.2 | 2.79 | -123.9 | yes |
| **fused+dtcm+slideh** | the same, head over a sliding window | **148,656** (min 146,336, max 154,790) | **46.5** | **2.68** | -123.9 | **shipping** |
| break | negative control: output scale 1% off | 329,944 | 103.1 | 5.96 | -40.0 | REJECTED, as it must be |

Output against the plain kernel's, bit for bit, on the board (column `exact_vs_base` in
`docs/benchmarks/data/daisy-seed3/nam-bench-final-sweep.csv`): `fused+dtcm` and `fused+dtcm+slideh` match in all 4800
samples; `break` in none, which is why it is rejected.

### 5.2 The step that tried the NAM Core layout and the sliding windows (2026-10-17, one build before the final code)

Evidence: `docs/benchmarks/data/daisy-seed3/nam-bench-first-sweep.csv`; the same command with the extra variants.

| variant | what | cycles/block | % budget | ESR dB | kept |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| base | plain kernel | 329,980 | 103.1 | -123.9 | baseline |
| fused+dtcm | fused tiles, state in DTCM | 154,912 | 48.4 | -123.9 | reference |
| slidel | sliding window on the four dilation-1 layers | 154,555 | 48.3 | -123.9 | no: 0.23% faster, 1.9 KB more flash |
| slideh | sliding window on the head | 151,010 | 47.2 | -123.9 | **yes: 2.5% faster** |
| slide | both | 150,934 | 47.2 | -123.9 | no: 76 cycles (0.05%) better than slideh alone |
| a2fast | NAM Core's `a2_fast` layout, state in DTCM | 208,343 | 65.1 | -123.3 | **no: 34% slower** |
| a2fast-axi | the same, state in AXI SRAM | 214,332 | 67.0 | -123.3 | no |
| break | negative control | 330,044 | 103.1 | -40.0 | REJECTED, as it must be |

Output against the plain kernel's, bit for bit, on the board (column `exact_vs_base` in
`docs/benchmarks/data/daisy-seed3/nam-bench-first-sweep.csv`): `fused+dtcm`, `slidel`, `slideh` and `slide` match in all
4800 samples; `a2fast` and `a2fast-axi` in only 175 (the sum order differs, the ESR is still -123.3 dB); `break` in
none.

The code for `slidel` and `a2fast` is not in this release: neither earned its place. They are described in section 9.

### 5.3 The sweep of the code before that (2026-10-16)

| variant | what | cycles/block | % budget | ESR dB | kept |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| base | plain kernel | 329,947 | 103.1 | -123.9 | baseline |
| dtcm | object in DTCM only | 320,987 | 100.3 | -123.9 | no: 2.7% |
| fused | 3 outputs x 4 frames, repacked weights, direct stores | 172,871 | 54.0 | -123.9 | no, not alone |
| **fused+dtcm** | | **154,896** | **48.4** | -123.9 | yes |
| fused+dtcm+lto | and `-flto` | 153,951 | 48.1 | -123.9 | no: 0.6%, and it costs a build-system change |
| fused+dtcm+fast | and `-ffast-math` | 166,803 | 52.1 | -122.5 | no: slower and less exact |
| fused+dtcm+o2 | image compiled `-O2` instead of `-O3` | 671,622 | 209.9 | -123.9 | no: 4.3 times slower |

All of these matched the plain kernel in all 4,800 samples except `fused+dtcm+fast` (`-ffast-math`, 202 of 4,800 equal).

### 5.4 What each step bought, in the first experimental tree (2026-10-16)

| step | cycles/block | note |
|---|---|---|
| plain | 351,737 | |
| + branch-free activation | 316,526 | -10% |
| + fused 3-output tiles, repacked weights | 244,399 | -31% on its own |
| + object in DTCM | 235,017 | -4%: the fused kernel is sensitive to where its memory is, the plain one is not |
| + epilogue constants in locals, frames unrolled | 202,984 | |
| + residual stored straight into the next ring | 163,366 | -20%: no `x` array, no per-layer copy |
| the same, rewritten cleanly (final tree, `fused+dtcm`) | 154,896 | the cleaner code compiled better |
| 8 frames per tile | 164,817 | the compiler spills registers; no gain over 4 |
| 2 frames per tile | 190,094 | |
| tap loop specialised on kernel size | 184,231 | worse: bigger code |
| bias and mixin folded into the start of the sum | 155,945 | -4.5% against 163,366, ESR -124.0 dB; **not adopted**, see section 9 |
| 3 taps per pass, loads first | 197,255 | worse |
| compiler pre-RA scheduler (`-fschedule-insns -fsched-pressure`) | 163,366 | no change |
| image `-O2` / `-Os` instead of `-O3` | 330,476 / 600,792 | the kernel depends on `-O3`'s unrolling and interleaving |

Where the plain kernel's cycles went (**measured** with the DWT's CPI, load-store and folded-instruction counters around
each
tap pass): 4.93 cycles per multiply-add inside the tap loops, which were 56% of a block; the rest was activation
branches, the
per-layer copy into the rings, and the residual. Moving the plain kernel's memory to DTCM changed it by only 2.5%, so it
was
not waiting for memory: it was issuing too many instructions.

## 6. The whole chain, with audio

The `nam-chain-b32` image runs, in one audio callback at 32 samples and 48 kHz: **gate, drive, A2-Lite, limiter**, from
a
built-in test input to both outputs. Measured 2026-10-17, final code, audio on for 36 s:

| | result |
|---|---|
| late blocks / overrunning blocks | **0 / 0** |
| whole callback, mean | **66.43% of budget** |
| whole callback, worst one-second window | **69.28%** |
| the A2-Lite stage alone | 47.08% |
| the other three stages together (arithmetic: 66.43 - 47.08) | about 19 points |
| warm-up guard reading before audio starts | 65.7% |

- In the same session, the chain with only the fused kernel (without the sliding head) gave 67.73% mean, 70.11% worst,
  and
  48.10% for the A2-Lite stage: the head window is worth about 1.3 points of total CPU.
- The three-stage chain without the amp (gate, drive, limiter), measured on this tree's blocks 2026-10-16: 18.7% mean
  and
  18.9% worst at block 32; 18.6% / 18.9% at 48; 18.5% / 18.8% at 64. About 1.3% is the gate, 5.3% the drive and 12.0%
  the limiter.
- The built-in test input is a fixed signal, not a guitar. The A2-Lite's cost does not depend on the signal (the kernel
  has no
  data-dependent branches), and this release's limiter costs the same on any signal.

The chain fits the Seed's internal flash, so no bootloader, QSPI flash or SDRAM is needed. It also has about a third of
the CPU
left over (**inference** from the 69.3% worst window: 30.7% free).

## 7. Memory

**Measured** from the linker's own memory report (`make -C hosts/daisy` writes `build/daisy/SIZES.md`):

| image | flash (of 131,072 B) | DTCM (of 131,072 B) |
|---|---|---|
| `nam-b32` (amp alone) | 96,664 B (73.7%) | 124,564 B (95.0%) |
| `nam-parity-b32` | 94,676 B (72.2%) | 124,564 B (95.0%) |
| **`nam-chain-b32`** (the chain) | **128,464 B (98.0%)**, 2,608 B spare | **124,564 B (95.03%)**, 6,508 B left for the stack |

- The A2-Lite images need libDaisy built `-Os` (about 20 KB smaller): at `-O2` the amp alone is 8 KB over the flash and
  the
  chain 15 KB over.
- **Stack high-water mark, measured.** Amp bench image (model run from the main loop, no audio): 1,912 to 1,944 bytes
  used of the
  6,508. Chain image with audio on (the interrupt callback shares the stack), 40 one-second windows: **2,896 bytes used,
  3,612 bytes never touched (55%)**.
- Only about 2.6 KB of flash is spare in the chain image. Any further feature would need the Daisy bootloader with QSPI
  or SRAM
  execution (**estimate** of what it would take: not tried).
- **Which image ran.** Built on a Mac with GCC 15.3.1, `seed3-nam-chain-b32.bin` is 128,464 bytes with sha256
  `15db1229cf0274545a8584c5d5b61067a1cebc5af7e68277a7adfd1dba7f7178`: the image that was on the board for the chain run.
  The
  The same code built in CI with the same compiler release but its Linux (x86_64) build is 128,456 bytes: 8 bytes
  different. We
  have not found why. So compare the size and the flash percentage across machines, not the hash.

## 8. Round-trip latency

**Measured**, with AUDIO OUT 1 (pin 18) wired to AUDIO IN 1 (pin 16). The Seed writes a one-sample click and finds it
coming back.
Each row is 56 to 57 clicks over 14 s with **zero jitter** (every click gave the same lag to 0.01 sample), peak -8.4
dBFS,
noise about -103 dBFS:

| block | round trip (samples) | round trip (ms) | 2 x block | rest (converters) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16 | 49.33 | 1.028 | 32 | 17.33 |
| 32 | 81.33 | 1.694 | 64 | 17.33 |
| 48 | 113.33 | 2.361 | 96 | 17.33 |
| 64 | 145.33 | 3.028 | 128 | 17.33 |

The lag is `2 x block + 17.33` samples at every block size: two blocks of buffering plus 0.361 ms of converter filter
delay.

With effects in the path, block 32, 72-sample limiter look-ahead (the default), **measured**:

| path | round trip |
|---|---|
| limiter only | 169.33 samples = 3.528 ms |
| gate + drive + limiter | 182.16 samples = 3.795 ms |

The limiter adds 88 samples (its look-ahead plus 16 samples for half its true-peak filter); the drive's filters add
12.83.
Those two images are built `-Os` to fit the flash, so their CPU is not comparable with the `-O3` figures.

The round trip with the A2-Lite in the path was **not measured**. **Inference:** the model works on each sample from the
past only, with no look-ahead, so it should add no delay and the chain should round-trip in about 182 samples (3.8 ms)
at
block 32. The image prints `latency 88 samples` as the delay its stages declare, which is the limiter's alone.

## 9. What did not help

All **measured** (tables in section 5):

- **NAM Core's `a2_fast` layout, ported to the M7: 208,343 cycles against 154,912, 34% slower** (65.1% of budget against
  48.4%; 214,332 in AXI SRAM). We ported its structure from `NAM/wavenet/a2_fast.cpp`: interleaved three-float columns,
  one tap at a
  time over the whole block, the partial sums kept in memory between taps. Reading (**inference**): each tap pass loads
  3
  history and 3 partial-sum words and stores 3, for 9 multiply-adds, and a multiply-add does not overlap a load on this
  core, so
  the round trip through memory costs more than holding 12 accumulators in registers. Two deliberate deviations: we kept
  this file's ring lengths (the original's power-of-two rings would need more than the 128 KB of DTCM), and the tap loop
  is a
  template on 6 or 15 as in the source. It is not bit-identical to the plain kernel (the sum order differs) but passes
  the
  accuracy gate at -123.3 dB. This says the layout is not the better one **for this core**, not that it is slow
  elsewhere.
- **A sliding window over the four dilation-1 layers: 0.23% faster** (154,912 to 154,555), for 1.9 KB more flash out of
  the 3 KB
  left in the chain image. Only 33 of the 156 taps are on those layers. Combined with the head window the gain vanishes
  (150,934 against 151,010). The estimate we had made beforehand was 5% to 8% for sliding windows; the measurement was
  2.5% for
  the head and nothing for the rest.
- **`-O2` instead of `-O3` for the image: 2.0 to 4.3 times slower** (330,476 against 163,366 in the first tree; 671,622
  cycles, 209.9% of budget, against 154,896 in the later one), and `-Os` 3.7 times slower (600,792 against 163,366).
  The kernel depends on `-O3`'s unrolling and interleaving; do not lower the optimisation level of the amp image.
- **The inexact fold** (bias and mixin folded into the start of the sum, residual taken from `x + bias`): 4.5% fewer
  cycles
  (155,945 against 163,366 in that tree, ESR -124.0 dB) but the output differs from the plain kernel in 4,573 of 4,800
  samples.
  The error against the float64 reference is unchanged, but we kept the rule that the shipping kernel is bit-identical
  to the
  plain one, so it was not adopted.
- **`-ffast-math`**: slower (166,803 against 154,896) and less exact (-122.5 dB).
- **`-flto`**: 0.6% faster, not worth the build-system change. **DTCM alone** (without the fused tiles): 2.7%.
- **8 frames per tile**: no gain (164,817 against 163,366), the compiler spills. **2 frames**: 190,094.
- **ITCM** (code in the instruction-tightly-coupled RAM) was not tried: the stock linker script has no section placed
  there. The
  code runs from the I-cache.
- **CMSIS-DSP routines**: `arm_conv_f32` and `arm_mat_mult_f32` take whole sequences and are scalar float loops on an M7
  without
  Helium; none does a 3-in 3-out dilated tap with a ring mirror, and the micro-benchmark says the loads are the cost,
  which a
  library call does not change. Not used.

## 10. What is untested

- **Estimates that were never measured:** a tile of 8 frames with hand-scheduled `vldm` loads would save about 8%
  (**estimate**; the compiler's version spilled). A 4-tap group on the head would need 33 live floats and spill
  (**estimate**).
- **Block sizes other than 32 for the amp.** Only block 32 was run for the amp images. The kernel is bit-identical
  across block
  sizes on the Mac, but its CPU at 16, 48 or 64 was not measured on the board.
- **Real playing.** The amp and chain images use a built-in input. Nothing was played through them with a guitar, and no
  one
  has judged the sound. The accuracy claim is ESR against the float64 reference on noise, not a listening test.
- **Long runs.** The longest chain run was 36 s (40 windows for the stack). Heat and long-term stability were not looked
  at.
- **One board and one compiler.** Another Seed3, a Seed 2, a different GCC, or a different libDaisy commit may differ,
  especially where the flash is 98% full.
- **The round trip with the amp** (section 8).
- **Splitting the model across two chips** (one chip per half of the layers, over SAI) was considered and not built,
  because one
  core was enough.
- **Operating systems.** The flashing and measurement tools were written and used on macOS. The firmware build is plain
  `make`
  and CI builds it on Linux (`.github/workflows/daisy.yml`); the tools have not been run on Linux or Windows.

## 11. How to reproduce it

You need a Daisy Seed3, `arm-none-eabi-gcc` 15.3.Rel1 (other versions may overflow the flash), `dfu-util`, `make`,
`git`, `curl`,
`python3` with `numpy`, and `clang++`.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/squatch-stack/squatch-dsp && cd squatch-dsp

hosts/daisy/fetch-libdaisy                   # libDaisy at the pinned commit, with the two patches
make -C hosts/daisy -j4                      # all images; build/daisy/SIZES.md has flash and RAM (section 7)
grep nam-chain-b32 build/daisy/SIZES.md      # about 128,460 bytes, 98.0% of the flash (section 7)

hosts/daisy/tools/fetch-nam-model            # NAM Core's A2.nam, checked against its sha256
export SEED3_SERIAL=<the board's USB serial>  # see hosts/daisy/README.md
```

Put the board in its bootloader once (hold BOOT, tap RESET, release BOOT). Then:

1. **The amp alone (section 4, 5.1)**:
   `hosts/daisy/tools/nam_bench.py --selftest --only 'base,fused+dtcm,fused+dtcm+slideh'`. It builds, flashes and
   measures each
   variant and the negative control and writes `build/daisy/nam-bench/<time>/results.md` and `.csv`. Expect 148,656
   cycles for
   `fused+dtcm+slideh` and `break` to be REJECTED. Your cycles should match to within a fraction of a percent if the
   compiler is the
   same.
2. **Accuracy on the parity image**: `hosts/daisy/tools/flash.py build/daisy/bin/seed3-nam-parity-b32.bin`, then
   `hosts/daisy/tools/nam_check.py`. It prints the number of bit-identical samples against the same kernel on the Mac,
   and the ESR
   against the float64 reference (expect about -123.9 dB, largest error about 5.4e-08).
3. **The chain with audio (section 6)**: flash `build/daisy/bin/seed3-nam-chain-b32.bin` and run
   `hosts/daisy/tools/serial_capture.py 40 chain.txt`. Read the `cpu`, `nam` and `blocks=... late=... over=...` lines:
   `late` and `over`
   must stay 0.
4. **Round trip (section 8)**: wire AUDIO OUT 1 (pin 18) to AUDIO IN 1 (pin 16), flash `seed3-latency-b32.bin`, and read
   the
   `LATENCY` line.
5. **Stack and memory**: the `# stack:` line from the bench image; `build/daisy/SIZES.md` for the rest.
6. **The weights header** needs no board: `hosts/daisy/tools/nam_to_header.py build/nam-model/A2.nam | diff -
   hosts/daisy/nam/a2lite_weights.hpp`
   prints nothing.

The host-side tests (`make test`) check the kernel is bit-identical across block sizes and the tools' guards, without a
board.

<!-- SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT -->
# Squatch Tuner

A guitar and bass tuner core that reads a string to a tenth of a cent, built as a software
strobe. Portable C++17, header-only, no dependencies. It has fixed-size buffers and never
allocates or locks in the audio path, so the same code can run on a Daisy Seed (Cortex-M7), an
ESP32-S3, a Pi 5 LV2 plugin, a desktop plugin and a WebAssembly AudioWorklet.

Measured numbers, with how they were measured and where it fails, are in [RESULTS.md](RESULTS.md).
It is developed here, in squatch-dsp's `blocks/tuner/`, and also published on its own as
[squatch-tuner](https://github.com/squatch-stack/squatch-tuner), with a
[browser demo](https://squatch-stack.github.io/squatch-tuner/). The
`TunerBlock` adapter (`include/squatch/dsp/blocks/tuner.hpp` at the top of the repo) puts it
behind the common `Block` interface, and its hosts are in the top-level `hosts/`.
The docs site has a chapter explaining the design and comparing it with other tuners and methods.

## How it works

```text
input (any rate) -> decimate to ~12 kHz -> history -> MPM every 5.3 ms: which note?
                                       \-> strobe bank, every sample: how far off?
                                             -> stiffness-aware fit -> reading
```

1. **Coarse: which note.** The McLeod Pitch Method (normalised square difference) finds the
   period. It runs every hop until a note is found, then every fourth hop to check the note.
2. **Fine: how far off.** This is a software strobe. Each partial k of the note is mixed down
   with a reference at k times the note's frequency, from one 32-bit phase accumulator. It is
   then low-passed by two boxcars a whole number of periods long, which null every other
   partial exactly. The drift rate of each partial's phase is its frequency error, found by a
   weighted least-squares line fit over a sliding window. A parabola fit reads the drift at the
   newest point, so a gliding note is followed without lag. That correction is shrunk by its
   own significance.
3. **Stiffness.** Real strings are stiff, so partial k sits at k·f0·√(1+Bk²). The fit estimates
   B per note and reports the fundamental itself, not the sharp average of the harmonics.
   Measured on real DI, MPM alone reads 2 to 6 cents sharp for this reason. B is the string's,
   so it is learned while the note is young and loud (50 ms to 2 s, within 30 dB of its peak)
   and then held.
4. **Robustness.** It handles these problem cases:
   - Partials that disagree with the rest (hum, a sympathetic string) are weighted down
     smoothly, so the number never flips between two partials. If they still disagree by more
     than 3 cents, the number is withheld rather than shown.
   - Octave slips in both directions are caught in the first half second of a note: upwards by
     the coarse stage, downwards when the odd partials of the reference are empty. After that a
     note is re-named only by a new pluck.
   - Readings are withheld once a note has decayed into the room's hum and noise floor.
   - Hum cannot start a note once a real note has been heard, and nothing starts without a
     pluck at a note's tail unless it is within 20 dB of that note and above 70 Hz.
   - Strings ringing together (a hard pluck rings the other open strings) can still start a
     note: a pitch the coarse stage keeps returning at lower clarity, checked against it.
   - A steady test tone present from power-on still reads.
5. **Polyphonic strum check** (`poly.hpp`). The tuning is known, so each string gets its own
   strobe channels at its target pitch.

The display gets two readings. `hz` follows the string, glide included, and drives the strobe
animation. `steadyHz` is averaged over the window, read a quarter of the way from its centre to
the newest point, and drives the number and needle.
`strobeTurns[k]` is each partial's phase, for drawing the strobe.

## Use

```cpp
#include <squatch/tuner/tuner.hpp>

static squatch::tuner::Tuner tuner;   // ~128 kB, keep it off the stack

void setup(float sampleRate) {
  squatch::tuner::TunerConfig c;
  c.sampleRate = sampleRate;           // any rate; decimated internally towards 12 kHz
  c.minHz = 38.0f;                     // 27 for a 5-string bass (B0)
  tuner.configure(c);                  // not real-time safe: builds tables
}

void audioCallback(const float* in, int n) {
  tuner.process(in, n);                // real-time safe, any block size
  const auto& r = tuner.reading();
  if (r.valid) show(r.midi, r.cents, r.steadyHz, r.strobeTurns);
}
```

## Layout

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `include/squatch/tuner/` | the core: `tuner.hpp` (mono), `poly.hpp` (strum check), `strobe.hpp`, `phase_slope.hpp`, `partial_fit.hpp`, `period.hpp` (MPM, YIN), `level.hpp`, `decimator.hpp`, `nco.hpp`, `history.hpp`, `common.hpp` |
| `tests/test_core.cpp` | unit tests, built with AddressSanitizer and UBSan; one test counts heap allocations during `process()` (must be zero) |
| `bench/` | the measurement harness: synthetic plucked strings with known truth, real DI evaluation, polyphonic strums, CPU cost; baselines (YIN, MPM, MPM + phase vocoder) behind the same front end |
| `bench/quality/` | the quality suite: the display path the apps use (TunerBlock, 30 reads a second, the release hold) over synthetic notes with exact truth and real DI with an offline reference, scored for accuracy and steadiness on every platform (`make tuner-quality`, see its README) |
| `results/` | raw output of `make results`, which RESULTS.md summarises |
| `docs/screens/` | screenshots of the live page |

The hosts are at the top of squatch-dsp:

| Path (from the repo root) | What |
|---|---|
| `hosts/common/` | host layer any front end can reuse: `display.hpp` (note name, steady and fast cents against a run-time A4); `latest.hpp` forwards to the core's lock-free handoff, `include/squatch/dsp/latest.hpp`; `tuner_host.hpp` and `tuner_publisher.hpp` (the live tuner's real-time step and JSON line, shared by the JACK and CoreAudio hosts); `tone_gen.hpp` (the exact sine) |
| `hosts/jack/` | `squatch-tuner-live`, the tuner behind a JACK input (Linux, the Pi), and `squatch-tone`, an exact test tone |
| `hosts/coreaudio/` | the same two programs for macOS, on CoreAudio directly: no JACK, only system frameworks |
| `hosts/web/` | `serve.py` (standard-library bridge: page + Server-Sent Events) and the strobe page |
| `hosts/wasm/` | the browser demo: the core as WebAssembly in an AudioWorklet, the same page with its own input bar, and its tests (`make wasm-test`) |
| `hosts/tests/` | the host layer's tests (ThreadSanitizer) |

## Build, test, measure

In this directory:

```sh
make test      # unit tests (ASan + UBSan); the top-level `make test` runs them too
make all       # tests and the bench programs
make results   # every number in RESULTS.md; needs the Guitar-TECHS DI files (see RESULTS.md)
make lint      # lizard: CCN <= 10, <= 60 lines, <= 5 parameters per function
```

The hosts build from the repo root: `make live` (CoreAudio on macOS, JACK elsewhere), and `make test` runs the host tests,
including the CoreAudio host's audio path against a test tone, with no audio device.

There are no dependencies to fetch: a C++17 compiler is enough. The bench uses only the
standard library.

## Live on a Raspberry Pi

`hosts/jack` runs the core behind a JACK input and `hosts/web/serve.py` streams its readings to
the strobe page in any browser on the network. RESULTS.md, "Live on the Pi 5", has the numbers
from a Pi 5 with a USB audio interface.

```text
capture_1 -> jackd (48 kHz, 64 x 3) -> squatch-tuner-live
     JACK realtime thread: Tuner::process() -> Latest<Frame>     (no allocation, locks or I/O)
     main thread, 30 times a second: newest Frame -> one JSON line on stdout
  -> serve.py: page + /events (Server-Sent Events) + /clock + POST /a4 -> browser
```

```sh
make live                                             # needs libjack-jackd2-dev
python3 hosts/web/serve.py -- build/squatch-tuner-live --input 1
build/squatch-tone 110                                # an exact test tone on playback_1
```

## Live on a Mac

On macOS `make live` builds the same two programs on CoreAudio. They link system frameworks only
(`otool -L` shows `/System` and `/usr/lib`), so nothing needs installing, and the options and the JSON
lines are the JACK host's.

```sh
make live
build/squatch-tuner-live --list-devices               # every device: channels, rate, which are the defaults
build/squatch-tuner-live                              # the default input device, channel 1
build/squatch-tuner-live --device umc --input 2       # a device by (part of) its name, channel 2
build/squatch-tone 110 --device umc --port 1          # an exact tone on that device's output 1
python3 hosts/web/serve.py -- build/squatch-tuner-live
```

- The first run asks, once, whether your terminal may use the microphone. If that was refused the input is
  digital silence, and the tuner says so on stderr after two seconds.
- It uses a device as it is: it never changes the Mac's default devices, a buffer size or a sample rate.
  `--out thru` needs one device with both inputs and outputs (an interface); a Mac's microphone and its
  speakers are two devices.
- `capMs` and `tin` come from the device's reported latency, not a loopback measurement.
- `make live LIVE_BACKEND=jack` builds the JACK version on a Mac that has JACK.

- The number and needle show `steadyHz`; the strobe drifts at the fast reading. Rows are
  partials 1, 2 and 4, so a fine error shows first on the bottom row.
- A4 is shared by every viewer (430 to 450 Hz). The polyphonic strum check is not exposed.
- The footer measures input-to-screen latency across the Pi's and the viewer's clocks, and
  shows the Pi's CPU.

## Porting notes

- **Daisy Seed (STM32H750, Cortex-M7 480 MHz).** Use the core as is. It needs single-precision
  floats in the per-sample path, plus a few hundred double operations per second in the fits,
  which the M7's FPU handles in hardware.
- **ESP32-S3.** Its FPU is single precision only. The fit's double sums run in software, so a
  `float` build of `PhaseSlopeWindow` is the first port task. The MPM inner loop should go
  through ESP-DSP's dot product. RESULTS.md has the estimates.
- **Plugins and Pi.** Wrap `Tuner` in the plugin framework.
- **Web.** Done: `hosts/wasm` compiles the same headers with Emscripten and calls `process()`
  from the AudioWorklet's 128-frame callback (`make wasm`, `make wasm-test`).

## The standalone repository

[squatch-tuner](https://github.com/squatch-stack/squatch-tuner) is the easy-to-embed copy: the
same files in a flat layout (`include/`, `bench/`, `tests/`, `hosts/`) plus the built demo in
`docs/`. It is written from this repository by `tools/export-public tuner`, never edited by
hand: its `EXPORTED` file lists a SHA-256 per file and the squatch-dsp commit they came from,
and its CI fails if a file there differs from that list or from squatch-dsp's main branch.

## Licence

MIT, like the rest of squatch-dsp (`LICENSE` at the repository root).

================================================================================
FILE: blocks/tuner/RESULTS.md    [Docs: Squatch Tuner: measured results]
